content.p: "Peckerwood" began as an insult. The Anti-Defamation League describes it as a slur aimed at white people that was taken up by members and associates of white supremacist prison gangs, who now wear it as a badge of honour. The word now covers three things: a prison subculture, a loose set of local gangs that call themselves Peckerwoods, and a vocabulary that spread from cell blocks to the streets.

No single organisation is described under the name. The Anti-Defamation League's 2022 assessment of white supremacist prison gangs says that various gangs in several states call themselves Peckerwoods, and that some prison systems use the word as a generic category for a white supremacist security threat group. The cases that have reached court, in North Texas in 2018 and in the San Fernando Valley in 2024, concern drug trafficking and fraud at least as much as ideology.

The 2018 reporting by NewsOne explains the term as a reversal of "woodpecker", particularly the red-bellied bird with a patch of red feathers on its head, a nod to the older insult "redneck". Like that word, the outlet wrote, it is a slur for poor, uneducated white men. In the later Los Angeles case, the Spokesman-Review reported that the gang's name came from an insult that was applied to white inmates in California's prisons.

The ADL says the men who live inside the subculture call themselves "peckerwoods" or simply "woods", and that women who are part of it call themselves "featherwoods" or "feathers". In a given prison, the group's members are often collectively known as "the woodpile". A poem that circulates in many versions, and that the ADL quotes in a version by a member of the Aryan Brotherhood of Texas, opens with the line "We're peckerwood soldiers, down for our cause." The ADL's profile reads the whole performance as pride: white inmates presenting themselves as soldiers standing together against everyone else.

Members also use shorthand. The ADL's list of codes includes "WMFW", which it expands as a profane phrase ending in "Wood". It also records a hand sign associated with Peckerwoods, in which one hand forms a "P" and the other a "W", and says the gesture is especially common in California, where Peckerwood street gangs are frequently found.

A study by the sociologists David Pyrooz of the University of Colorado Boulder and Scott Decker of Arizona State University gives a rare view from inside. The researchers spent nine months in two of the oldest prisons in Texas and interviewed 802 inmates, about half of them gang members, each close to release. One interviewee in the university's account joined the Peckerwoods at 19 for protection, during a period of rising race riots that the university's account links to the highly publicized murder of a Black man by white supremacists in East Texas. "It's hard in here for a white guy," he told his interviewer.

The researchers found that about half of prison gang members first join after they arrive in custody, often looking for protection, cultural identity or belonging. They also found that gangs rarely deliver the protection recruits expect, and that gang members are far more likely to be victims of violence than non-members. Pyrooz called the idea of "blood in, blood out" a myth, adding that most men who joined in prison had left the gang by the time they were released. Decker said that prison gangs no longer rule with the iron fist they once did, and that membership in rigid top-down groups such as the Aryan Brotherhood was waning while looser, clique-like gangs were growing.

The ADL argues that most white supremacist prison gangs are organised crime groups first and hate groups second. White supremacy, it says, serves to bind members together and make it less likely that one will inform on the group, and that practical purpose helps explain why such gangs can make deals with non-white gangs, typically Hispanic ones, when money is at stake. The degree to which individual members hold the ideology varies widely, from fully committed believers to men who show nothing more than crude racism.

The Texas branch of the family shows the pattern. The ADL's profile of the Aryan Brotherhood of Texas says it came out of the desegregation of Texas prisons and the dismantling of the "building tender" system, in which staff used other inmates, mostly white ones, to keep order. Black, Hispanic and white gangs flourished in the resulting uncertainty. In the early to mid-1980s most members of two white gangs, the Aryan Society and the Aryan Brothers, united as the Aryan Brotherhood of Texas, and others left out of the merger later helped found the rival Aryan Circle. The ADL says the Texas group committed 13 murders in 1984 and 1985 alone. It also notes that, despite the name, the Texas gang has no connection to the original Aryan Brotherhood, which formed in California in the 1960s.

The ADL describes the "peckerwood" subculture as having begun among white inmates in the South and West who belonged to or associated with racist prison gangs, and as having since spread to most prisons and onto the streets. A Texas inmate who joins is often back outside quickly: the ADL says the average felon in Texas serves only about three years, so men recruited in prison are soon back on the streets.

In 2018 a federal grand jury in North Texas indicted 57 members of several white supremacist gangs on drug trafficking and kidnapping charges, the Justice Department announced, according to NewsOne. The outlet described the Peckerwoods in that case as a newer group trying to make a name, an unaffiliated prison-based gang that, prosecutors said, had coalesced out of the Aryan Brotherhood of Texas. NewsOne quoted the Southern Poverty Law Center as calling them Aryan Brotherhood "wannabes who do the gang's bidding", whose service to the larger gang built their own prestige. Some members wore T-shirts showing a woodpecker on a motorcycle with the line "Peckerwoods, this wood don't burn."

Authorities seized 190 kilograms of methamphetamine, 31 guns and $376,587 in cash, NewsOne reported. The gangs were accused of trafficking methamphetamine mainly through North Texas from October 2015 to April 2018, and four suspects were accused of kidnapping a man they believed had stolen money, cutting off his index finger as punishment.

The ADL's 2022 assessment later summed up the wider case. Between 2015 and 2018, it says, dozens of people with ties to white supremacist prison gangs, among them five named groups (the Aryan Circle, the Aryan Brotherhood of Texas, the Peckerwoods, the Soldiers of Aryan Culture and the Dirty White Boys) moved drugs and guns across Texas, including more than 1,600 kilograms of methamphetamine. The ADL reports that a multi-agency investigation led to arrests and, eventually, convictions of more than 150 gang members. According to authorities, defendants received 1,820 years in federal prison in total, and the Justice Department called it the largest prosecution focused on white supremacist prison gangs.

On Wednesday 2 October 2024 federal prosecutors in Los Angeles unsealed an indictment against 68 alleged members and affiliates of the Peckerwoods, a white supremacist gang based in the San Fernando Valley. The Spokesman-Review said twelve alleged members were charged with racketeering and another 56 defendants with conspiring to distribute drugs. Law and Crime reported that 29 of the 68 were arrested that day and 13 were already in custody. The racketeering conspiracy statute at the centre of the case is the same one, the outlet noted, that was used against organised crime in the 1970s. The case carries a statutory maximum of life in federal prison.

According to the indictment, as reported, the conduct ran from December 2016 to September 2024. Prosecutors alleged that members sold methamphetamine, heroin and fentanyl, robbed drug dealers, and took part in "smash-and-grab" thefts. They also alleged more sophisticated crimes: identity theft and bank fraud, including fraudulent loan applications signed for people held in California state prisons, with the gang then collecting part of the proceeds. Law and Crime gave one example from April 2021, in which a defendant said he was a self-employed "artist/writer" with a gross income of nearly $250,000 and received a loan of $20,833. Drugs were mailed to customers, and payments went through Zelle and CashApp, prosecutors said.

Prosecutors also described the group's ideology. They said members used Nazi tattoos, graffiti and iconography, including swastikas, the number 88 as code for "Heil Hitler", and images of Nazi aircraft. In a private Facebook group, according to the indictment, one member wrote during the protests that followed the police killing of George Floyd in June 2020: "I wish all the blacks and all the cops would just kill ALL of each other." Even so, the Spokesman-Review reported, the gang's primary concern, in prosecutors' account, was money.

The indictment alleged an alliance with the Aryan Brotherhood, which the report called the dominant white gang in the California prison system, and that its imprisoned members took a "tax" on proceeds. Two alleged Aryan Brotherhood members, Paul John Pichie and Michael Vitanza, were charged with conspiring to traffic drugs. The indictment also lists dozens of unnamed conspirators who were not charged, and it makes clear, the report said, that defendants communicated with prisoners using contraband cellphones. Law and Crime added that the gang was allied with the Mexican Mafia, a prison gang the outlet said holds sway over most Latino street gangs in California.

In a statement, U.S. Attorney Martín Estrada said the gang's "violent white-supremacist ideology and wide-ranging criminal activity pose a grave menace to our community." The case followed earlier racketeering prosecutions of the Aryan Brotherhood, in which, the Spokesman-Review wrote, a jury convicted a man described at trial as a member of the gang's three-man "commission" and two co-defendants of murder in aid of racketeering in 2024. The report said that plan to move them to more restrictive federal prisons had stalled because the Bureau of Prisons refused to accept the California inmates.

The indictment is an accusation, and the defendants are presumed innocent unless and until convicted. The pages opened for this account report no verdicts, pleas or sentences in the San Fernando Valley case.

The ADL's state-by-state listing shows how widely the name travels. It records Peckerwoods in Nevada, Nebraska and New Mexico; Peckerwood Midwest, a Missouri-based prison and street gang; the Inland Empire Peckerwoods, started in 1995 by a California inmate who recruited in the Minnesota system; the International Peckerwood Syndicate, formed in 2005 in the Oregon prison system and also known as the Insane Peckerwood Syndicate; and the Branded Peckerwood Family, a small gang in Connecticut. The report says various white supremacist gangs call themselves Peckerwoods in different states; it does not describe them as one organisation.

That fragmentation makes the name a poor guide to what any one group does. The cases that reached court in 2018 and 2024 turned on the particular conduct alleged against the particular defendants, not on the word on their tattoos or T-shirts.
